intro.title: Discover The Great Arch of the Defense
intro.description:
The Great Arch of the Defense (La Grande Arche de la Défense), also known as the 'Modern Arc de Triomphe', is one of France's most iconic modern architectural masterpieces. Designed by Danish architect Johan Otto von Spreckelsen, it was completed in 1989 to commemorate the 200th anniversary of the French Revolution.

This magnificent white marble structure stands 110 meters high, 110 meters wide, and 110 meters deep, forming a massive cubic 'arch'. It perfectly aligns with Paris's historical axis—from the Louvre Pyramid, through the Champs-Élysées, to the Arc de Triomphe, and finally to La Grande Arche.

The Arche is not just an architectural masterpiece but also a multifunctional space containing office areas, exhibition spaces, and an observation deck at the top. From the deck, visitors can enjoy 360-degree panoramic views of Paris, including the iconic historical axis.

As the centerpiece of the La Défense business district, this monument symbolizes France's modernization and vision for the future while maintaining respect for history and tradition.

knowledge.title: The Story of The Great Arch

sections.title: History & Construction
sections.content:
The Great Arch of the Defense project began in 1982 as part of France's 'Grands Travaux' (Great Works) program initiated by President François Mitterrand. The goal was to create a modern triumphal arch perfectly aligned with Paris's historical axis.

Danish architect Johan Otto von Spreckelsen won the international design competition in 1983. His design was a massive white marble cube with a hollowed center forming an 'arch'. The official inauguration took place on July 14, 1989, coinciding with the 200th anniversary of the French Revolution.

sections.title: Architectural Significance
sections.content:
La Grande Arche is not just a building but a symbol. It represents France's vision for the future while maintaining respect for history and tradition. The structure's pure lines and monumental scale embody modernist ideals.

The location of the Arche is deeply meaningful—it sits at the western end of Paris's historical axis, which begins at the Louvre, continues through the Tuileries Garden, Champs-Élysées, Arc de Triomphe, and finally reaches La Défense. This spatial arrangement reflects France's continuity from history to modernity.

sections.title: Architectural Features
sections.content:
La Grande Arche is an astounding engineering feat:

1. Dimensions: 110m high, 110m wide, 110m deep—a perfect cube
2. Materials: White Carrara marble, glass, and steel
3. Weight: Approximately 300,000 tons
4. Design: Hollow cube forming a 'gate' shape
5. Observation deck: Open-air deck at the top, accommodating hundreds

The north and south wings of the building are enclosed office spaces, while the east and west faces are open 'arches'. This design is both functional and rich in symbolism.

sections.title: About the Architect
sections.content:
Johan Otto von Spreckelsen (1929-1987) was a renowned Danish architect and designer. He was known for his minimalist and classical modernist style.

Other notable works by Spreckelsen include St. Bernard's Church in Copenhagen. His design philosophy emphasized pure geometric forms, high-quality materials, and careful handling of light. Unfortunately, Spreckelsen passed away in 1987 and did not live to see the completion of the Grande Arche. The project was completed by French architect Paul Andreu.

route.title: Recommended Itinerary
route.overview: Start from Arc de Triomphe, take Metro Line 1 to La Grande Arche (10 minutes), visit the Arche and observation deck (1.5 hours), enjoy panoramic views of Paris from the top, then explore La Défense modern architecture district (1 hour). Total trip takes about half a day.

Get off at 'La Défense - Grande Arche' station, follow signs to the Grande Arche
Visit the base of the Arche, admire the monumental scale and white marble facade
Take the elevator to the top observation deck, enjoy 360-degree panoramic views of Paris
From the deck, identify Paris's historical axis: Arc de Triomphe, Champs-Élysées, Louvre
Visit exhibition spaces inside the Arche (if available)
Exit the Arche, explore other modern buildings in La Défense district
Visit the nearby 'Le Delta' and La Défense Plaza
Choose from numerous restaurants in La Défense for lunch or dinner
Take the Metro back to Paris city center, or enjoy the night view of the Arche at dusk

officialManagement.title: About The Great Arch of the Defense
officialManagement.text:
The Great Arch of the Defense (La Grande Arche de la Défense) is one of France's most iconic modern architectural masterpieces, designed by Danish architect Johan Otto von Spreckelsen and completed in 1989 to commemorate the 200th anniversary of the French Revolution.

This magnificent white marble structure is located at the heart of Paris's La Défense business district, perfectly aligned with the historical axis from the Louvre to the Arc de Triomphe. The Grande Arche is not just an architectural masterpiece but also features an observation deck offering visitors 360-degree panoramic views of Paris.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
faq.subtitle: Common questions about The Great Arch of the Defense — location, transport, tickets and the observation deck.

items.q: Where is The Great Arch of the Defense located?
items.a: The Great Arch of the Defense (La Grande Arche de la Défense) stands in Puteaux, in the Hauts-de-Seine department (92), on the western edge of Paris. Address: 1 Parv. de la Défense, 92800 Puteaux, France.

items.q: How do I get to the Grande Arche de la Défense by public transport?
items.a: Take Métro line 1 to the La Défense – Grande Arche station, or RER A to La Défense. From the Arc de Triomphe the journey takes about 10 minutes; the Arche is a short walk from the station across the esplanade.

items.q: Is the Grande Arche the same as the Arc de Triomphe?
items.a: No. The Arc de Triomphe (1836) is the 19th-century arch at Place Charles de Gaulle, while the Grande Arche is a modern 110-metre hollow cube completed in 1989. Both mark the ends of Paris's historic axis (Louvre – Champs-Élysées – Arc de Triomphe – La Défense).

items.q: When and why was the Grande Arche built?
items.a: The Grande Arche de la Défense was designed by Danish architect Johan Otto von Spreckelsen and inaugurated on 14 July 1989, on the 200th anniversary of the French Revolution.

items.q: Can you go up to the top of the Grande Arche?
items.a: The rooftop observation deck (Le Toit de la Grande Arche) is ticketed and its opening schedule may change by season or for maintenance. Please confirm current opening days, hours and ticket availability on official channels before your visit.

items.q: Is visiting the Grande Arche free?
items.a: The public esplanade, the La Défense plaza and the monument's exterior are free to view. Access to the rooftop observation deck and the exhibitions inside is charged.

items.q: What can you see from the top of the Grande Arche?
items.a: From the 110-metre-high terrace you get a 360° panorama over the La Défense business district, the Seine valley and Neuilly-sur-Seine, with the Arc de Triomphe, the Champs-Élysées and the Louvre aligned along the historic axis to the east.

sources.nearby: The Great Arch stands at the western end of Paris's historic axis and at the centre of the La Défense business district. A short walk across the esplanade takes you to the CNIT and Les Quatre Temps; looking east along the axis you can see the Arc de Triomphe, the Champs-Élysées and the Louvre. Puteaux, Neuilly-sur-Seine, Courbevoie and Suresnes all border La Défense, making the district easy to combine with a wider visit to Hauts-de-Seine.

cards.text: Public restrooms are usually available in large public buildings, office lobbies, shopping centres and Metro stations around La Défense, often free or low-cost and frequently with accessible and baby-changing facilities. Station concourses are a convenient stop when transferring between lines.

cards.title: Parking
cards.text: Parking nearby is dominated by paid underground or multi-storey public car parks, plus short-stay on-street bays. Park-and-ride (P+R) lots beside stations suit the 'park here, take the Metro' pattern. Spaces tighten on weekends and during events, so arrive early or use public transport.

cards.title: Food & Drink
cards.text: Options range from bistros and cafés to bakeries, quick-service kitchens, supermarket grab-and-go and delivery pick-up points. For a lighter budget, consider a bakery or supermarket meal. If you sit down to eat, check the menu and prices first — French lunch service peaks around 12:00–14:00 and dinner from 19:00.

cards.title: Supermarkets & Everyday Shops
cards.text: Supermarkets, convenience stores and pharmacies sit mostly in building podiums and shopping malls — handy for water, snacks and essentials. Many close earlier on Sundays and some public holidays, so check opening hours for the day you plan to visit.

cards.title: Fuel & EV Charging
cards.text: Drivers can refuel at petrol stations along main roads or inside large car parks. Electric vehicles can charge at public charging networks or chargers inside shopping-centre car parks. Before a long return trip, check your fuel level or battery state; charger types and rates are displayed on site.

stories.title: History, Stories & Fun Facts
stories.subtitle: How a hollow cube built in ten years crowned the world's grandest urban sightline — with the legends, debates and numbers behind it.

timeline.text: French President François Mitterrand and the La Défense planning authority (EPAD) launch the 'Tête Défense' international competition, to give the historic axis a monument worthy of the 20th century.
Danish architect Johan Otto von Spreckelsen's entry — an immense hollow cube — is chosen from hundreds of submissions.

Construction begins on a site crossed by roads, rail and the RER. Differences over budget and schedule lead Spreckelsen to hand over the project; French architect Paul Andreu takes charge of the completion.
Spreckelsen dies without seeing the cube rise. Andreu's team carries his concept through to the very end.
The arch is inaugurated on the bicentenary of the French Revolution under the name 'Grande Arche de la Fraternité', as heads of state gather in Paris for the G7 summit.
The towers fill with offices, the esplanade becomes one of Europe's largest pedestrian spaces, and the rooftop is developed into the panorama and exhibition deck known as 'Le Toit'.

stories.title: A window open to the world
stories.text: Spreckelsen always described his cube not as an arch but as a 'window open to the world'. Stand inside and look east: the Louvre, the Tuileries, the Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe all line up in the frame.

stories.title: A slight, deliberate twist
stories.text: The Grande Arche is not perfectly parallel to the historic axis — its own axis deviates by roughly 6 degrees. Whether this was a perspectival trick, a constraint of the underground railway works, or both, is still debated. Either way, the subtle rotation gives the cube real depth when approached from the Champs-Élysées.

stories.title: A cube tall enough for Notre-Dame
stories.text: The hollow opening of the arch is about 110 metres high and spans the full width of the cube — big enough that Notre-Dame Cathedral could stand beneath it.

stories.title: A district that 'defends' Paris
stories.text: La Défense takes its name from the statue 'La Défense de Paris' (1883), commemorating the city's defence in 1870–71. More than a century later, the district still guards the western end of the capital's great axis.
